{{Short description|Result on periodic sequences}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2025}}

In [[combinatorics on words]], '''Fine and Wilf's theorem''' is a fundamental [[Theorem|result]] describing what happens when a long-enough [[String (computer science)|word]] has two different periods (i.e., distances at which its letters repeat).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511566097/type/book |title=Combinatorics on Words |series=Cambridge Mathematical Library |date=29 May 1997 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-59924-5 |editor-last=Lothaire |editor-first=M. |edition=2 |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511566097}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Karhumäki |first=Juhani |title=Combinatorics of Words |url=https://www.math.utu.fi/en/home/karhumak/pdf/combwo.pdf |access-date=23 November 2024}}</ref> Informally, the conclusion is that such words <math>w</math> have also a third, shorter period. If the periods and length of <math>w</math> satisfy certain conditions, then this third period can equal <math>1</math>. In this case then, the theorem's conclusion is that <math>w</math> is a power of a single letter. The theorem was introduced in 1963 by [[Nathan Fine]] and [[Herbert Wilf]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Fine |first1=N. J. |last2=Wilf |first2=H. S. |date=1965 |title=Uniqueness theorems for periodic functions |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1965-016-01/S0002-9939-1965-0174934-9/ |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=109–114 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1965-0174934-9 |issn=0002-9939|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is easy to prove, and has uses across [[theoretical computer science]] and [[symbolic dynamics]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-59136-5 |title=Handbook of Formal Languages |date=1997 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-59136-5 |isbn=978-3-642-63863-3 |editor-last1=Rozenberg |editor-last2=Salomaa |editor-first1=Grzegorz |editor-first2=Arto }}</ref><ref name=":0" />
[[File:Herbert Wilf.jpg|thumb|235x235px|Herbert Wilf, who introduced the theorem alongside Nathan Fine]]

== Statement ==
The two most common phrasings of Fine and Wilf's theorem are as follows:<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" />

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>w</math> be a word with periods <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> (i.e., distances at which its letters repeat). If the length of <math>w</math> is at least <math>p + q - \gcd(p,q)</math>, then <math>w</math> also has period <math>\gcd(p,q)</math>.
}}{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>u,v</math> be nonempty words. If the infinite words <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> have a common prefix of length <math>\mid u\mid +\mid v\mid -\gcd(\mid u\mid ,\mid v\mid )</math>, then <math>u,v</math> are powers of a common word.
}}

It is folklore that an [[Sequence|infinite sequence]] <math>(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}</math> having two periods <math>h</math> and <math>k</math> has also <math>\gcd(h,k)</math> as a period.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Shallit |first=Jeffrey |title=Fifty Years of Fine and Wilf |url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~shallit/Talks/vu3.pdf |access-date=23 November 2024}}</ref> Indeed, by [[Bézout's identity]], there are [[integer]]s <math>r,s \ge 0</math> satisfying <math>rh-sk=\gcd(h,k)</math> or <math>rk- sh =\gcd(h,k)</math>. In the first case, we always have <math>a_n = a_{n+rh} = a_{n+rh-sk} = a_{n+\gcd(h,k)}</math>. And in the second, we always have <math>a_n = a_{n+rk} = a_{n+rk-sh} = a_{n+\gcd(h,k)}</math>.

Fine and Wilf's theorem refines this result only by bounding the length of the sequence <math>(a_n)</math> to some large-enough finite value such that the third period must still arise. The finite bound of Fine and Wilf is optimal. Indeed, consider <math>w := aaabaaa</math>. Then <math>w</math> has periods <math>4</math> and <math>6</math>, since <math>w = aaab \cdot aaa = aaabaa \cdot a</math>. By Fine and Wilf's theorem, <math>w</math> would also have period <math>\gcd(4, 6) = 2</math> if its length were at least <math>4+6-\gcd(4,6)=8</math>. In fact, the length of <math>w</math> is <math>7</math>, only one short of this threshold, and <math>w</math> fails to have this short period <math>2</math>.

== Proof ==
We prove the second phrasing of the theorem above. The proof comes from,<ref name=":1" /> and is closely related to the [[extended Euclidean algorithm]], much like the proof of [[Bézout's identity]].

Let <math>u,v</math> be nonempty words over an [[Alphabet (formal languages)|alphabet]] <math>\Sigma</math>. We first reduce to the case <math>\gcd(| u |, | v | ) = 1</math>: If instead we have <math>|u| = dp</math> and <math>|v| = dq</math>, with <math>d>1</math>, <math>\gcd(p,q)=1</math>, we consider <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> as elements of <math>(\Sigma^d ) ^+</math>. That is, we view them as words over the alphabet <math>\Sigma^d</math> whose letters are words of length <math>d</math> in the original alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>. With respect the larger alphabet <math>\gcd(|u|,|v|)=1</math>, and so proving the result for this case will suffice.

So let <math>p:=|u|</math> and <math>q:=|v|</math> with <math>\gcd(p,q)=1</math>. Suppose that <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> have a common prefix of length <math>p+q-1</math>. Assume further (by symmetry) that <math>p>q</math>, and consider the image shown below. Here the positions of the words <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> are numbered <math>1,2,..,p+q-1</math>. The vertical dashed line indicates how far the words <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> can be compared.
[[File:FineAndWilfProcedure.png|thumb|382x382px|The procedure used in our proof of Fine and Wilf's theorem.]]
The arrow describes a procedure, the purpose of which is to fix the values of new positions to be the same as a given value of an initial position <math>i_0\in[1,..,q-1]</math>. By our premises, the value of the position computed as follows:<math display="block">i_0 \mapsto i_0 + p \mapsto i_1 \equiv i_0 + p \pmod q,</math>where <math>i_1</math> is reduced to the interval <math>[1,...,q]</math>, gets the same value as that of <math>i_0</math>. So the procedure computes <math>i_1</math> from the number <math>i_0</math>. Since <math>\gcd(p,q)=1</math>,  <math>i_1</math> differs from <math>i_0</math>. If <math>i_1</math> differs from <math>q</math> as well, the procedure can be repeated. The claim is: The new positions obtained will always differ from all the previous ones. Indeed, if <math display="block">i_0 + np \equiv i_0 + mp \pmod q</math>with <math>n,m\in[0,q-1]</math>, then necessarily <math>n=m</math>, since <math>\gcd(p,q)=1</math>.

Now, if the procedure can be repeated <math>q-1</math> times, then every position in (the first repetition of) <math>v</math> will get covered, meaning that these'll all get the same letter as the initial one at position <math>i_0</math>. But this implies that <math>v</math> is a power of a single letter, and thus so is <math>u</math>. Hence, this would complete the proof.

But the procedure ''can'' be repeated <math>q-1</math> times if we choose <math>i_0</math> such that <math>i_0 + (q-1)p \equiv q \pmod q</math>.  If this holds, then all the values <math>i_0 + jp \pmod q</math> for <math>j=0,...,q-2</math> differ from <math>q</math>. Clearly, such an <math>i_0</math> can be found.

== Variants ==
Often the following weakening of Fine and Wilf's theorem is formulated:<ref name=":1" />

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>u,v</math> be nonempty words. If the infinite words <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> have a common prefix of length <math>\mid u \mid + \mid v \mid</math>, then <math>u,v</math> are powers of a common word.
}}

This variant can be proved using a simplified version of the above argument. It is often strong enough in application.<ref name=":1" />

Another reformulation removes the emphasis on the words' "left-hand-sides" (i.e., the requirement for <math>uuu\cdots</math> and <math>vvv\cdots</math> to agree from the start). This statement therefore requires only that <math>uuu\cdots</math> has a different periodic presentation than the trivial one as a repetition of <math>u</math>s. To write it down formally, let <math>\ell(w_1,w_2)</math> denote the maximal length of a common factor of the words <math>w_1</math> and <math>w_2</math>. Then<ref name=":1" />

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>u,v</math> be nonempty words. If <math>\ell (uuu\cdots,vvv\cdots)\ge \mid u\mid +\mid v\mid -\gcd(\mid u\mid ,\mid v\mid )</math>, then the primitive roots of <math>u,v</math> are conjugates.
}}

Variants of the theorem have also been introduced that look at abelian periods.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Karhumäki |first1=Juhani |last2=Puzynina |first2=Svetlana |last3=Saarela |first3=Aleksi |chapter=Fine and Wilf's Theorem for k-Abelian Periods |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2012 |volume=7410 |editor-last=Yen |editor-first=Hsu-Chun |editor2-last=Ibarra |editor2-first=Oscar H. |title=Developments in Language Theory |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-31653-1_27 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=296–307 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-31653-1_27 |isbn=978-3-642-31653-1}}</ref> (i.e., consecutive blocks in words that are not necessarily identical, but [[anagram]]s of each other). There are also ways to apply the theorem to [[continuous function]]s having multiple periods<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

== Generalisations ==
Fine and Wilf's theorem has been generalised to work with words having more than two periods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Constantinescu |first1=Sorin |last2=Ilie |first2=Lucian |date=11 June 2005 |title=Generalised fine and Wilf's theorem for arbitrary number of periods |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S030439750500023X |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |series=Combinatorics on Words |volume=339 |issue=1 |pages=49–60 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2005.01.007 |issn=0304-3975|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4" /> For instance, for three periods <math>p_1 < p_2 < p_3</math>, the appropriate bound is<math display="block">\frac{1}{2}\left(p_1 + p_2 + p_3 - 2\gcd(p_1, p_2, p_3) + h(p_1, p_2, p_3)\right),</math>where <math>h</math> is a function related to the [[Euclidean algorithm]] on three inputs<ref name=":5">{{Citation |chapter=Sturmian Words |date=2002 |title=Algebraic Combinatorics on Words |pages=45–110 |editor-last=Lothaire |editor-first=M. |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/algebraic-combinatorics-on-words/sturmian-words/D7AD019B0546AE7258C6B38B13F14CAE |access-date=23 November 2024 |series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/cbo9781107326019.003 |isbn=978-0-521-81220-7|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4" />

The result has also been investigated with respect to "[[partial word]]s",<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berstel |first1=Jean |last2=Boasson |first2=Luc |date=28 April 1999 |title=Partial words and a theorem of Fine and Wilf |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0304397598002552 |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=218 |issue=1 |pages=135–141 |doi=10.1016/S0304-3975(98)00255-2 |issn=0304-3975|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which are allowed to contain "don't care" positions called holes. Holes match each other and all other letters. The following has been proved:<ref name=":4" />

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = There exists a computable function <math>L(h,p,q)</math> such that, if a word <math>w</math> with <math>h</math> holes and periods <math>p,q</math> has length <math>\ge L(h,p,q)</math>, then <math>w</math> also has period <math>\gcd(p,q)</math>.
}}

== Relation to Sturmian Words ==
Let <math>p,q</math> be [[Coprime integers|coprime]]. Fine and Wilf's Theorem allows for words of length <math>p+q-2</math> to have periods <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> without being a power of a single letter. In fact, given <math>p</math> and <math>q</math>, such a word always exists.<ref name=":1" /> Moreover, it is binary and unique (up to renaming its letters).

The proof of this claim follows the proof given above. Indeed, in that proof, the letters in the positions of the shorter word were fixed using the procedure. The procedure could be applied in all but one case, namely when the position was <math>q</math>. Now there are ''two'' positions wherein the procedure cannot be applied, viz. <math>q</math> and <math>q-1</math>. Accordingly, we are free to choose the letters occurring in two positions of the shorter word, but as soon as we do this, every other position is fixed. Since we want a word that's not a power of a single letter, our only choice (modulo the letters' names) is to put different letters in the two positions we have control over. Uniqueness follows from the fact that every other position is fixed.

The words so obtained are the finite [[Sturmian word]]s.<ref name=":1" /> These words admit many characterisations;<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /> the above discourse gives a way to compute them.

== Applications ==
One application of Fine and Wilf's theorem is to [[string-searching algorithm]]s.<ref name=":4" /> For instance, the [[Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm|Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm]] finds all occurrences of a pattern <math>p</math> in a text <math>t</math> in time bounded by <math>O(|p|+|t|)</math>. It compares <math>p</math> to a portion of <math>t</math> beginning at a position <math>i</math> and, if a mismatch is found, shifts <math>p</math> rightward depending on where the mismatch occurred.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cormen |first1=Thomas H. |title=Introduction to algorithms |last2=Leiserson |first2=Charles Eric |last3=Rivest |first3=Ronald Linn |last4=Stein |first4=Clifford |date=2022 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-04630-5 |edition=4th |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts London, England}}</ref> The worst-case for the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm comes from "almost-periodic" words, the idea being that – in this case – long sequences of matching letter can occur without a complete match. It turns out that such words are precisely the maximal "[[counterexample]]s" to Fine and Wilf's theorem (i.e., the finite [[Sturmian word]]s, described in the previous section)<ref name=":4" />

Fine and Wilf's theorem can also be used to reason about the solution sets of [[word equation]]s.<ref name=":1" />
